content.study:
Current-law identity
BNSS s. 173 governs information in cognizable cases within Chapter XIII - Information to the police and their powers to investigate. The provision must be read with its enacted sub-sections, provisos, explanations, the BNSS First Schedule where classification or trial forum is relevant, and BNSS s. 172, BNSS s. 174. Historical concordance: CrPC s. 154.

Procedural meaning and legislative purpose
Criminal procedure is a sequence of safeguards, not a collection of isolated powers. This section allocates a procedural step to the police, Magistrate, trial court, Sessions Court or High Court and places conditions around its exercise. The mischief addressed is identified from the statutory text and Chapter setting; the court should not add a condition that the legislature did not enact or remove a safeguard that the text requires.

Mandatory application checklist
1. Identify the proceeding, procedural stage and order sought.
2. Confirm whether the investigation, inquiry, trial, application or appeal was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. If so, begin with BNSS s. 531(2)(a) and test whether the saved CrPC route governs.
3. Quote the exact operative words of s. 173, including every condition, proviso and explanation.
4. Identify the competent criminal court, territorial rule, statutory sanction or classification requirement.
5. Map each material fact to the statutory condition it proves or fails.
6. State the immediate remedy and the standard for interference.

Evidence and constitutional control
The procedural record remains subject to Articles 14, 20, 21 and 22 of the Constitution. The party asserting a factual foundation bears the ordinary burden under BSA s. 104; BSA s. 106 is limited to facts especially within a person's knowledge after the foundation is established. Electronic records must be separately tested under BSA s. 63 for the applicable certificate and production requirements. BSA admissibility does not cure an unlawful arrest, search, remand or other BNSS defect.

Courtroom method
In a written submission, state the current section first, identify the stage and forum, reproduce only the necessary statutory language, address the transition rule, apply each condition to the record, answer the principal objection, and request a precise order. Do not treat a police report as proof of guilt, an arrest as a conviction, a charge as a finding, or a procedural irregularity as automatically destroying the entire prosecution.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective and Doctrinal Foundation
sections.body:
BNSS s. 173 regulates information in cognizable cases within Information to the police and their powers to investigate.
Read the provision purposively but begin with its enacted text and the Chapter structure.
The constitutional background includes fair procedure, personal liberty and judicial accountability under Articles 14, 21 and 22.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos and Connected Provisions
sections.body:
Deconstruct every clause of BNSS s. 173; do not replace the provision with a CrPC summary.
Read it with BNSS s. 172, BNSS s. 174. A connected section may define the condition, forum, time limit or remedy without replacing this section.
Use historical concordance only to explain development, never as the current citation.

sections.heading: Mandatory Procedural Ingredients and Stage Test
sections.body:
First ingredient: the proceeding must be at the statutory stage addressed by s. 173.
Second ingredient: the competent officer or court must possess the relevant jurisdiction and power.
Third ingredient: each express condition, notice, reason, time limit, record or hearing requirement must be satisfied.
Fourth ingredient: the requested consequence must follow from the proved procedural breach or compliance; state the exact order sought.

sections.heading: BSA 2023 Burden and Electronic Evidence Checkpoints
sections.body:
BSA s. 104 supplies the ordinary burden framework; do not shift the initial burden merely by invoking s. 106.
BSA s. 106 applies to a fact especially within knowledge only after the party relying on the legal proposition establishes the necessary foundation.
Where electronic material is tendered, separately examine relevance, authenticity, integrity, source and BSA s. 63 certificate requirements.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Forum, Limitation and Transition
sections.body:
For proceedings under the post-1 July 2024 regime, cite BNSS s. 173 and verify the First Schedule or special statute where applicable.
For a matter pending immediately before commencement, apply BNSS s. 531(2)(a) and identify the saved CrPC procedure before addressing merits.
Check the applicable BNSS or special-statute limitation rule and calculate the remedy period from the actual order or event.

examples.title: Example 1 - Conditions satisfied
examples.body: A proceeding is at the stage governed by s. 173; the authorised officer or court records each statutory reason, follows the required notice and hearing path, and acts within jurisdiction. The order is tested against the section and its connected provisions.

examples.title: Example 2 - Boundary defect
examples.body: The decision-maker applies s. 173 without checking the procedural stage, the s. 531 savings rule or an express statutory condition. The advocate identifies the missing condition and seeks the precise procedural remedy rather than asserting an automatic result unsupported by the Act.

hypotheticals.question: Whether the order under BNSS s. 173 is sustainable and what immediate relief is available.
hypotheticals.analysis: 1. Identify the stage and whether the proceeding was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. 2. State the exact test in s. 173. 3. Verify jurisdiction, notice, reasons, time limits and hearing requirements. 4. Test the electronic record separately under BSA s. 63. 5. Grant only the remedy supported by the proved defect, such as modification, release, disclosure, remand correction, quashing where maintainable or appellate interference.

distinctions.title: BNSS s. 173 and its connected procedure

rows.right: Do not import the neighbour's test automatically
Historical CrPC numbering is concordance only

misconceptions.trap: Citing only the old CrPC number for s. 173.
misconceptions.correction: Use BNSS s. 173 for the current regime and mention the historical number only when the transition or comparison requires it.

misconceptions.trap: Treating procedure, offence and proof as one issue.
misconceptions.correction: Analyse BNSS procedure, BNS or special-statute liability, and BSA proof as separate legal layers.

misconceptions.trap: Using BSA s. 106 to avoid proving foundational facts.
misconceptions.correction: The asserting party must first establish the legal and factual foundation; special knowledge does not erase the initial burden.

cases.name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
cases.facts: The petitioner sought registration of information disclosing a cognizable offence.
cases.issue: Whether registration is mandatory when information discloses a cognizable offence.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Registration is mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence, subject to the limited preliminary-inquiry framework recognised by the Constitution Bench.
cases.holding: The Court directed compliance with mandatory registration and confined preliminary inquiry to recognised categories.
cases.relevance: Use only where s. 173 concerns information, investigation or a connected pre-cognizance step; do not treat this case as authority for every BNSS provision.

cases.name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
cases.facts: The case concerned arrest and detention for an offence carrying imprisonment up to seven years.
cases.issue: Whether arrest and remand may be authorised mechanically in a lower-punishment case.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Police must satisfy and record the necessity conditions for arrest, and Magistrates must not authorise detention mechanically.
cases.holding: The Court issued safeguards enforcing the discipline now reflected in the BNSS arrest framework.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 173 concerns arrest, custody, remand or liberty; otherwise identify a section-specific authority instead of forcing this case into the argument.

cases.name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
cases.facts: The Court addressed custodial violence and the absence of reliable arrest safeguards.
cases.issue: What minimum protections must accompany arrest and detention.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Arrest and custody require transparent documentation, accountability and safeguards protecting Articles 21 and 22.
cases.holding: The Court prescribed arrest and custody safeguards that inform the corresponding BNSS duties.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 173 directly engages arrest, custody, production or custody records; do not cite it as a substitute for the statutory text.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Provide a structured legal brief on BNSS s. 173 - Information in cognizable cases.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE AND JURISDICTION
Identify the procedural stage, competent forum, commencement status and precise order sought.

II. RULE
BNSS s. 173 governs information in cognizable cases. Read its clauses, provisos and connected provisions BNSS s. 172, BNSS s. 174; then test s. 531 savings.

III. APPLICATION
Map each fact to jurisdiction, statutory condition, notice, reason, time limit and evidentiary foundation. Test electronic records under BSA s. 63 and burdens under ss. 104-106.

IV. CONCLUSION
State whether the order stands, must be modified or requires a specific procedural remedy.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Draft written submissions on BNSS s. 173 - Information in cognizable cases.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. PROCEDURAL PROVENANCE
Set out the registration date, stage, orders and material relied upon.

II. STATUTORY SCHEME
Deconstruct BNSS s. 173, the Chapter setting, connected provisions BNSS s. 172, BNSS s. 174 and s. 531 savings.

III. MANDATORY INGREDIENTS
Address forum, jurisdiction, conditions precedent, notice, reasons, time limits, hearing and the statutory consequence.

IV. PRECEDENTS AND EVIDENCE
Use only verified authorities relevant to the proposition. Apply BSA ss. 63, 104-106 to digital and factual proof without shifting the initial burden improperly.

V. REBUTTAL AND PRAYER
Answer the transition, maintainability and merits objections, then seek the precise order supported by the record.

Statutory text strictly follows Act No. 46 of 2023, s. 173.

learningObjectives: Master the statutory procedure for recording information in cognizable offences under BNSS s. 173 (replacing Section 154 CrPC).
Understand the statutory codification of Zero FIR: registration irrespective of the territorial jurisdiction of the police station under s. 173(1).
Analyze the electronic FIR (e-FIR) framework and the mandatory requirement for physical/digital signature within three days under s. 173(1) proviso.
Examine the statutory Preliminary Enquiry mechanism under s. 173(3) for offences punishable between 3 to 7 years, requiring DSP prior permission within 14 days.
Evaluate remedies against police refusal to register an FIR: escalation to the Superintendent of Police under s. 173(4) and Magistrate under s. 175(3).
enhancement.definition: BNSS s. 173 establishes the statutory charter for receiving and recording information relating to cognizable offences. It mandates the registration of an FIR irrespective of territorial jurisdiction (Zero FIR), authorizes electronic information (e-FIR) subject to signature within three days, provides for a mandatory free copy to the informant, introduces a structured preliminary enquiry (within 14 days with DSP approval) for offences punishable between three to seven years, and enacts statutory remedies before the Superintendent of Police upon police refusal.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Access to justice, prompt state action, and statutory prevention of police gatekeeping in cognizable offences under Article 21 of the Constitution. The registration of an FIR is a mandatory statutory duty that activates the investigative machinery of the state.
statutoryFramework: Chapter XIII — Information to the Police and Their Powers to Investigate, BNSS s. 173.
Sub-section (1): Information given orally or by electronic communication; reduction to writing, reading over, and signing.
Proviso 1 to Sub-section (1): Zero FIR mandate — information to be recorded irrespective of the area where the offence was committed.
Proviso 2 to Sub-section (1): e-FIR signature requirement within three days before registration on record.
Sub-section (2): Mandatory furnishing of a free copy of the FIR to the informant or victim immediately.
Sub-section (3): Preliminary enquiry mechanism for offences punishable with 3 to 7 years (completed within 14 days with DSP permission).
Sub-section (4): Statutory remedy upon refusal of officer-in-charge: sending substance of information in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police.
essentialIngredients: Receipt of information disclosing the commission of a cognizable offence by an officer in charge of a police station.
Reduction of oral information to writing, reading over to the informant, and signature by the informant.
Zero FIR compliance: mandatory registration irrespective of territorial jurisdiction, with subsequent transfer to the competent police station.
e-FIR compliance: electronic information recorded and signed by the informant within three days.
Preliminary Enquiry threshold: permitted only for offences punishable with 3 to 7 years imprisonment, requiring prior permission of a DSP, and strictly time-bound to 14 days.
Immediate delivery of a copy of the recorded information free of cost to the informant.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 173 BNSS fundamentally modernizes the threshold of criminal investigation, replacing Section 154 of the 1973 Code. It statutorily codifies landmark procedural developments while introducing critical checks against misuse.

First, Section 173(1) explicitly enacts the concept of the **Zero FIR**. Historically, police stations frequently refused to register FIRs on the pretext of lack of territorial jurisdiction. Under Section 173(1), an officer in charge of a police station is statutorily bound to record information regarding a cognizable offence irrespective of where the crime occurred, initiate immediate urgent steps (such as medical examination or crime scene preservation), and subsequently transfer the record to the police station possessing territorial jurisdiction.

Second, Section 173(1) formally integrates **electronic communication (e-FIR)** into criminal procedure. A citizen may report a cognizable crime via email, portal, or electronic messaging. However, to prevent malicious or fictitious complaints, the proviso mandates that the electronic information shall be taken on record only after the informant signs it within three days.

Third, Section 173(3) introduces a revolutionary **Preliminary Enquiry (PE)** framework for offences punishable with imprisonment between three and seven years. To protect against frivolous or motivated complaints, the officer in charge may, with the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, conduct a preliminary enquiry to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists, or proceed directly to investigate where a prima facie case exists. The preliminary enquiry must be completed within an absolute statutory deadline of fourteen days.

Fourth, Section 173(4) provides the statutory escalation route: if an officer in charge refuses to register an FIR, the aggrieved informant may send the substance of the information in writing and by post to the Superintendent of Police, who may investigate personally or direct a subordinate investigation.
examples: Teaching illustration (Zero FIR in transit crime): A woman is assaulted inside an interstate bus travelling from City X to City Z. Upon arriving at City Z, she approaches the nearest police station. The officer refuses to register the complaint, claiming the assault occurred within City Y’s jurisdiction. The refusal is illegal. Under Section 173(1) proviso, the officer is mandated to register a Zero FIR, arrange immediate medical aid, and transfer the case to City Y.

Teaching illustration (e-FIR and 3-Day Signature Rule): A merchant reports an online cheating offence of ₹5,00,000 via the state police citizen portal on Monday at 10:00 AM. Under Section 173(1), the merchant must visit the police station or provide a digital signature verifying the complaint by Thursday 10:00 AM (within three days) for the e-FIR to be formally registered on record.

Teaching illustration (Preliminary Enquiry Compliance): An FIR is lodged alleging an offence carrying 5 years imprisonment. The police initiate a preliminary enquiry to ascertain prima facie truth. However, they continue the inquiry for 30 days without registering an FIR or obtaining DSP permission. The delay violates Section 173(3), entitling the complainant to seek a direction for registration from the Magistrate.
distinctions: BNSS s. 173 vs CrPC 1973 s. 154: BNSS s. 173 statutorily codifies Zero FIR, introduces e-FIR with a 3-day signature rule, and provides a statutory 14-day Preliminary Enquiry with DSP sanction for offences carrying 3–7 years.

BNSS s. 173 vs BNSS s. 174: Section 173 governs mandatory registration of information in cognizable offences, whereas Section 174 governs non-cognizable offences where police cannot investigate without an order from a Magistrate.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether the refusal of a Station House Officer to register an FIR for an alleged offence under Section 115(2) BNS (voluntarily causing hurt) without conducting a preliminary enquiry for 20 days is lawful.

Rule: Under Section 173(3) BNSS, a preliminary enquiry is permissible only for offences punishable between 3 to 7 years, requires prior permission of an officer not below DSP rank, and must be concluded within 14 days.
Application: The police failed to obtain DSP permission, and the preliminary enquiry exceeded the statutory ceiling of 14 days without registering the crime.

Conclusion: The inaction of the police violates BNSS Section 173; the informant is entitled to submit the complaint to the SP under s. 173(4) or apply to the Magistrate under s. 175(3) for an order directing registration and investigation.

keyTakeaways: Section 173 BNSS makes registration of cognizable offences mandatory across all police stations.
Zero FIR is codified: police cannot refuse registration on grounds of territorial jurisdiction.
e-FIR is recognized provided it is signed by the informant within three days.
Preliminary enquiry is restricted to offences punishable with 3–7 years and must conclude within 14 days with DSP approval.
